standard.title: Unique passphrases and password reuse risks
standard.description: Access multiple personal accounts using unique passphrases and explain the risks of password re-use
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can access their school account using a memorised password and explain why it should be easy to remember but hard for others to guess (AC9TDI4P08). They have a single-account security practice. They have not yet managed multiple accounts with different credentials, or understood the specific risk cascade that password reuse creates.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students access multiple accounts using unique passphrases and can explain why password reuse creates a risk cascade when one credential is compromised.

nodes.label: Why passphrases are stronger than passwords
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what makes a passphrase strong and why passphrases are more secure than short passwords
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two characteristics of a strong passphrase (length, unpredictability) and contrast with a weak password
nodes.typical_width: Explain that passphrases are longer sequences of words that are hard to guess but easier to remember than short complex passwords; describe what makes a passphrase strong (length, not a famous phrase, not personal info) and what makes it weak
wider: Compare how a brute-force attack works against a short complex password versus a long passphrase — explaining why length is more protective than character complexity alone
Investigate how password managers store multiple unique passphrases securely — and why using a password manager is better than reusing a memorable password

response_modes.reason: The passphrase strength reasoning (length beats complexity; unpredictability beats memorability) is counter-intuitive. Students need the reasoning made explicit — 'a longer random phrase takes exponentially longer to guess than a short complex one' — before they can apply it to evaluate their own credentials.

success_criteria: Explains at least two characteristics that make a passphrase strong
Contrasts a strong passphrase with a weak password example
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand what makes a credential strong cannot reason about the reuse risk in N2 — the cascade argument requires knowing that a compromised credential is now known to an attacker, and that requires understanding what 'compromised' means relative to credential strength.

nodes.label: The risk cascade of password reuse
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how reusing a password across multiple accounts creates a risk cascade when one account is compromised
nodes.minimum_width: Describe a scenario where the same password is used on two accounts; explain what an attacker can do if they discover that password
nodes.typical_width: Explain the full risk cascade: one account is compromised → attacker obtains the password → attacker tries the same password on other accounts → multiple accounts compromised; identify which types of accounts are most valuable to protect (banking, school, personal communications)
wider: Explain how credential stuffing attacks work — automated attempts to use a leaked username/password list against multiple websites — and why unique passphrases prevent them
Investigate a real-world example where a social media breach led to bank or email account compromise because users had reused credentials — without identifying specific individuals

response_modes.reason: The password reuse risk is abstract until students see the chain: one compromise → many compromises. Multiple concrete scenarios (social media + school + gaming + banking) where each account has a different consequence of compromise help students understand what is at stake at each link in the chain.

success_criteria: Explains that a compromised password can be used to access other accounts if the same password is reused
Identifies at least two accounts where this compromise would matter
